stances.claim: Trump's populism -- anti-black, anti-Asian, anti-migrant, anti-establishment -- jeopardizes two centuries of American libertarian struggle, and the danger is doctrinal as well as political because his three Scotus appointees have tilted the Court to a 6-3 conservative balance.

Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) was a hideous decision that denied citizenship to black slaves born in the US -- overturned only by the 13th and 14th Amendments, and CJ Taney plus the six majority justices are 'damned forever in US constitutional history.'

Brown v. Board of Education unanimously and triumphantly reversed Plessy v. Ferguson's separate-but-equal doctrine, holding that race-based separate facilities are inherently unequal under the 14th Amendment.

Miranda v. Arizona constitutionalized the police-warning regime for arrested crime suspects -- and the Philippines did one better by embedding Miranda rights directly in the Bill of Rights, where violation can lead to acquittal even if the accused is factually guilty.

Roe v. Wade's privacy-doctrine reading of the due-process clause has been repeatedly challenged but never overturned -- through Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (2016), and June Medical Services v. Russo (2020), where the right was narrowed but preserved.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-resilience tracking across four narrowing cases

stances.claim: Bush v. Gore (5-4) was heavily criticized for partisanship -- Bush's brother Jeb was Florida governor, Katherine Harris co-chaired Bush's FL campaign and headed the election body, and the five GOP-appointed justices voted solidly for Bush while the four Democrat-appointed lined up for Gore -- yet Gore conceded, in contrast to Trump's no-concession stance.

Gore's own framing -- 'there is something greater than me... The Supreme Court has spoken. Though I disagreed with the decision, I had the duty to respect and obey it' -- is the canonical concession ethic; and Gore's confirmation in the 2006 meeting that he would NOT have invaded Iraq/Afghanistan (his campaign promise), saving trillions that could have reduced extreme global poverty including the Philippines', is the most powerful counterfactual indictment of the Bush years.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-meeting disclosure + concession-ethic exemplar + alternate-history counterfactual

notable_anecdotes: The CJ-Gore 2006 meeting -- Gore's 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me... The Supreme Court has spoken. Though I disagreed with the decision, I had the duty to respect and obey it...' -- the most powerful concession-ethic exemplar CJ deploys against Trump's no-concession stance.

The Iraq/Afghanistan counterfactual -- CJ pressing Gore: 'Had you been president, would you have ordered the invasion of Iraq and Afghanistan?' Gore: 'No, never. That was my campaign promise.' CJ: 'Then, the US would not have spent trillions of dollars in those wars which you could have used to reduce extreme poverty in the world including ours, right?' Gore: 'Yes, yes, including the Philippines.'

The 13th-and-14th-Amendment doctrinal repair of Dred Scott -- 'CJ Roger Taney, and the six justices who voted with him were damned forever in US constitutional history' -- the strongest historical-damnation language CJ uses on named jurists.

PH-improves-on-US framing on Miranda -- 'We did better: Our Constitution, not just our courts, embedded these Miranda rights in its Bill of Rights' -- the rare CJ moment of constitutional pride placing PH ahead of the US.

Roe-v.-Wade's four-case narrowing arc (Casey 1992 → Carhart 2007 → Hellerstedt 2016 → Russo 2020) -- tracked as the resilient survival of an under-attack doctrine, written before Roe's eventual 2022 reversal.

The partisan-criticism catalog of Bush v. Gore -- Jeb Bush as Florida governor; Katherine Harris's dual role; the perfect appointment-party-line vote -- used to set up Gore's contrasting concession as the moral hero.
Closing teaser -- 'Next Sunday: Five contentious PH cases' -- sets up A188.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames Donald Trump's continuing populist rabble-rousing -- anti-black, anti-Asian, anti-migrant, anti-establishment -- as a jeopardy to two centuries of US libertarian struggle for social, racial, gender, and political equality, and traces that struggle chronologically through five Scotus decisions. First, Dred Scott v. Sandford (March 6, 1857, 7-2) held that black slaves born in the US were not 'citizens' but mere possessions -- a 'hideous decision' that the 13th and 14th Amendments had to overturn, and that 'damned forever' CJ Roger Taney and his six concurring justices. Second, Brown v. Board of Education (May 17, 1954, unanimous) reversed Plessy v. Ferguson (May 18, 1896, 7-1) by holding that the separate-but-equal doctrine in race-segregated schools violated the 14th-Amendment equal-protection guarantee -- separate facilities being inherently unequal. Third, Miranda v. Arizona (June 13, 1966) required police to advise crime suspects of their rights upon arrest -- and 'we did better': the 1987 PH Constitution embedded Miranda rights directly in the Bill of Rights, where violation can lead to acquittal even of the factually guilty. Fourth, Roe v. Wade (Jan 22, 1973, 7-2) read the abortion-privacy right out of the due-process clause; repeated challenges since 1973 narrowed it through Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (2016), and June Medical Services v. Russo (2020) but did not overturn it. Fifth, Bush v. Gore (Dec 12, 2000, 5-4) reversed a Florida SC manual-recount order, awarding Florida's 25 electoral votes and the presidency to George W. Bush by a very narrow 271-267 margin though Al Gore won the popular vote. The 5-4 was heavily criticized for partisanship -- Bush's brother Jeb was the Florida governor, Katherine Harris was both election-body head and co-chair of Bush's FL campaign, and the five GOP-appointed justices voted solidly for Bush against the four Democrat-appointed for Gore. In stark contrast to Trump's no-concession stance, Gore conceded -- and when CJ met him in 2006 during his PH visit, Gore explained: 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me... The Supreme Court has spoken. Though I disagreed with the decision, I had the duty to respect and obey it...' Pressed by CJ on whether he would have invaded Iraq and Afghanistan, Gore was quick: 'No, never. That was my campaign promise' -- confirming that 'the US would not have spent trillions of dollars in those wars which you could have used to reduce extreme poverty in the world including ours.' Gore chuckled: 'Yes, yes, including the Philippines.' CJ concludes that Trump's populism -- aided by his three conservative Scotus appointees who have tilted the balance to 6-3 -- endangers this libertarian struggle for equality. 'Next Sunday: Five contentious PH cases.'
